q-50139.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-10\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-10x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-10x+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =-10\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+Cx+D \\  & =-5{x}^{2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

q-50148.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
q-50148.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}={e}^{3x}.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{3x}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}\,{e}^{3x})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{e}^{3x}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

q-64254.knowledge_point: Calculating the Amplitude of an Simple Harmonic Oscillation
q-64254.source_problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with simple harmonic motion, is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+144y=0,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with a velocity of $8\,\text{m/s},$ find the amplitude of the oscillation.
q-64254.worked_solution:
The simple harmonic motion (SHM) equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.
$$

The general solution to the SHM equation can be written as

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ),
$$

where $R$ is the amplitude, and $ϕ$ is the phase. In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=144\,⟹\,\omega =12.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t+ϕ).
$$

We're given the initial condition $y(0)=0.$ Substituing this into the equation gives

$$
R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=0\,⟹\,ϕ=0.
$$

So our general solution reduces to

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡12t.
$$

We're told that the velocity is $8\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0,$ which means that ${y}^{′}(0)=8.$ Differentiating the general solution with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=12R\operatorname{cos}⁡12t.
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=8$ into the above gives

$$
8=12R\,⟹\,R=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the amplitude is $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{m}.$ The solution for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡12t.
$$

q-65167.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
q-65167.source_problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-2yz+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$
q-65167.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\text{ }i+(2xy-2z)\text{ }j+(-2y+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+(2(1)(-1)-2(1))\,j+(-2(-1)+1)\,k \\  & =1\,i-4j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$

q-65448.knowledge_point: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch and Vertical Shift of a Transformed Tangent Curve
q-65448.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13943521/assets/10912ded2166eb7ae28ee81c2936f008bf14eb288ec95969b822dd138be509d8.png)

The graph above shows the function $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(Bx)+D,$ where $B$ and $D$ are constants. What is $B+D?$
q-65448.worked_solution:
The period $T$ of the function is

$$
T=\pi -(-\pi )=2\pi .
$$

The formula for the period $T$ of the function $y=A\operatorname{tan}⁡(Bx+C)+D$ is given by 

$$
T=\frac{\pi }{B}.
$$

Applying the formula of the period, we get

$$
2\pi =\frac{\pi }{B}\,⟹\,B=\frac{\pi }{2\pi }=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the tangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $1$ unit up. Hence, $D=1.$

Therefore, $B+D=\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}.$

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+1.
$$

The parameter $D$ represents the vertical shift of the cotangent function. We see that the function has been translated by $3$ units down. Hence, $D=-3.$

Therefore, $B-D=(\frac{5}{4})-(-3)=\frac{5}{4}+3=\frac{17}{4}.$

Finally, the equation of the curve is

$$
y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{5x}{4})-3.
$$

Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }6}{\text{factor of }7}.
$$

q-85966.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Side Given the Rate of Change of the Volume
q-85966.source_problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14096050/assets/8e03226558b1dbb2e93d23947b0b05f3d8413dc35207bbe9b536e68108f40955.png)

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $3\,\text{cm}\text{/min},$ while the $5\,\text{cm}$ height does not change. If the volume of the rectangular prism is increasing at a rate of $15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $6\,\text{cm}$ in length and $2\,\text{cm}$ in width?
q-85966.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =2\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =15\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $z$ is not changing and $z=5,$ we get

$$
V=5xy.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5xy) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =5x(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5y(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =5(6)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+5(2)(-3) \\ 15 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})-30 \\ 45 & =30(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=6\,\text{cm},$ $y=2\,\text{cm}$ and $z=5\,\text{cm}.$

Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}(2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4{x}_{3}-2{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

q-89589.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Sums of Exponentials
q-89589.source_problem: Find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{4t}$ for $s>4.$
q-89589.worked_solution:

q-94283.knowledge_point: Calculating the Amplitude of an Simple Harmonic Oscillation
q-94283.source_problem:
The position $y(t),$ measured in meters, of a particle oscillating with simple harmonic motion, is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+8y=0,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the particle is initially at the origin with a velocity of $4\,\text{m/s},$ find the amplitude of the oscillation.
q-94283.worked_solution:
The simple harmonic motion (SHM) equation is

$$
{y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.
$$

The general solution to the SHM equation can be written as

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ),
$$

where $R$ is the amplitude, and $ϕ$ is the phase. In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=8\,⟹\,\omega =2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Thus, we have

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t+ϕ).
$$

We're given the initial condition $y(0)=0.$ Substituing this into the equation gives

$$
R\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ=0\,⟹\,ϕ=0.
$$

So our general solution reduces to

$$
y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

We're told that the velocity is $4\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0,$ which means that ${y}^{′}(0)=4.$ Differentiating the general solution with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=2\sqrt{2}R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=4$ into the above gives

$$
4=2\sqrt{2}R\,⟹\,R=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m}.$ The solution for $y(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\sqrt{2}t).
$$

q-94609.source_problem: Find the center of the elliptic cone $4(x-1)^{2}+10(y-4)^{2}={z}^{2}.$
q-94609.worked_solution:
The general equation of an elliptic cone with center at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is

$$
\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=\frac{(z-{z}_{0})^{2}}{{c}^{2}}.
$$

To find the center, we rewrite our equation in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4(x-1)^{2}+10(y-4)^{2} & =(z-0)^{2} \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{1/4}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{1/10} & =(z-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of an elliptic cone that has its center at $(1,4,0).$

q-99009.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
q-99009.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

q-99204.source_problem: Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum product of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is $108.$
q-99204.worked_solution:
Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}yz=2\lambda x \\ xz=2\lambda y \\ xy=2\lambda z\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}xyz=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,2,2) & =10\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =40 \\  & <f(6,6,6).\end{aligned}
$$
